why:
Fractional crystallization is the method defined for exactly this situation. Section 3.2.2 states that it is "a process wherein two or more soluble substances having widely different solubilities in the same solvent at room temperature are separated by crystallization" — two compounds, one solvent, different solubilities. A saturated solution of the mixture is cooled, the less soluble solute crystallises out first and is filtered off, and the mother liquor is then concentrated to crystallise the second solute.

The other three fail on what they are for. Crystallization (section 3.2.1) purifies a single crude solid from its impurities; it does not separate two compounds from each other. Distillation (section 3.3) separates liquids on a difference in boiling point, not solubility. Solvent extraction (section 3.4) needs two immiscible liquids and exploits a difference in the solubility of one solute between those two liquids, which is not the same as two solutes having different solubilities in one solvent.

Distillation under reduced pressure is used. Section 3.3.3 says so directly: liquids with a very high boiling point, or which decompose on heating, are purified by boiling them below their normal boiling point at a lowered pressure, and "In soap industry glycerol is separated from soap by using this technique." Glycerol is exactly such a liquid.

Fractional distillation is for two liquids whose boiling points differ only slightly (section 3.3.2), which is not the glycerol-soap case, and it would still mean heating glycerol to its normal boiling point. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (section 3.2) and soap is not an insoluble residue here. Crystallization purifies a crude solid by dissolving and re-depositing it, which does not address a high-boiling liquid.

Chromatography. Its definition in section 3.5 is the only one in the chapter that carries both halves of what the question asks: "Chromatography is a technique used to separate components of a mixture, and also purify compounds." Column chromatography in particular is described as separating the components of a loaded mixture into bands which are then collected separately and recovered by evaporating the solvent.

Steam distillation is not a technique this chapter teaches at all — the word does not occur outside this option list — so nothing supports it. Solvent extraction moves one solute from an aqueous layer into an immiscible organic layer; it is a transfer of a substance between two phases, not a general method for resolving a mixture into all of its components. Filtration only divides an insoluble residue from the filtrate and cannot resolve substances that are dissolved together.

Fractional distillation. Section 3.3.2 names this very pair: "Mixtures of acetone (b.p. 329 K) and methyl alcohol (b.p. 337.7 K); acetone and benzene (353 K) can be separated by fractional distillation." Acetone boils at 329 K and benzene at 353 K, and the vapours are passed through a fractionating column where repeated exchange between ascending vapour and descending liquid enriches the vapour in the more volatile acetone.

Simple distillation is ruled out by the chapter's own opening sentence for section 3.3.2: when the difference in boiling points of two liquids is not appreciable they cannot be separated using the simple distillation assembly. Distillation under reduced pressure is reserved for liquids of very high boiling point or which decompose on heating (section 3.3.3), and neither acetone nor benzene is such a liquid. Sublimation is a solid-to-vapour method and is not taught in this chapter; both components here are liquids.

This question asks which method does NOT work, so the answer is the one the chapter never offers: infrared light. Nothing in the chapter uses infrared radiation to visualise a chromatogram.

The other three are all stated methods and therefore all fail as answers. Section 3.5.1 says that components which are not coloured but are fluorescent "can be visualised under UV light", so ultraviolet light does work. The same section says the plate can be kept in a chamber containing a few iodine crystals, whose vapours are adsorbed by the components so that the spots appear brown, so an iodine chamber does work. It also gives ninhydrin sprayed on the plate as the spraying agent for amino acids, and section 3.5.2 repeats that colourless components "are observed under UV light or using a spraying agent", so a spraying reagent does work.
